newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Uighurs say China executes five, Beijing denies.
newsitem.headline: Uighurs say China executes five, Beijing denies.

text.p: An exile group said on Monday that China had executed five ethnic Uighurs who were accused of involvement in riots that rocked the country's predominantly Moslem northwest province of Xinjiang last month.
But Chinese officials in Xinjiang dismissed the allegation as "laughable".

"We know for sure that five people (Uighurs) were executed on March 20," Mukhiddin Mukhlisi, spokesman for the United National Revolutionary Front of East Turkestan, said at a congress of exile Uighur groups near the Kazakh capital Almaty.

Xinjiang officials said last week they had indicted six people, who could face the death penalty if convicted, in connection with anti-Chinese rioting in the province but said the case was not over yet.
Mukhlisi said the executions took place in the town of Yining, located near the Chinese-Kazakh border and scene of last month's disturbances which left nine dead and 198 wounded.
Exile groups said last month the Yining riots were sparked by the execution of about 30 Uighurs by the Chinese authorities.
A western traveller recently returned from the region said Yining was now calm.
But he added security was tight across Xinjiang province: "There are Chinese soldiers virtually everywhere you go."
Mukhlisi named one of those executed as Abdukhalil Abdulmedchit, saying he was a prominent leader of the rioting, but he could not name the other four.
Information from the region of inhospitable desert and remote mountain passes is difficult to verify. News often arrives days late from traders crossing the busy China-Kazakh border.
"We have close contacts with Xinjiang," said Kakharman Khozhamberdi, head of the Almaty-based Regional Uighur Association. "This is how we knew about the executions."

Mukhlisi's United National Revolutionary Front is one of several Uighur organisations fighting for an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, home to a majority of Turkic-speaking Moslems like the ethnic Uighurs.

The Front, the Regional Association of Uighurs and the Free Uighuristan movement met on Monday in the village of Kalinino, 15 km (nine miles) east of Almaty, at a congress aimed at uniting exile groups in Kazakhstan.

About 300 turned out from Kazakhstan and the neighbouring former Soviet states of Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan to pack a small cultural centre in the village, decorated with Islamic slogans written in Arabic. A Uighur mullah's call for independence won a storm of applause.
The ex-Soviet states neighbouring Xinjiang, which share the region's Turkic language, Islam and a nomadic past, have put flesh on Uighur dreams of independence.
Last year, the Xinjiang authorities cracked down on Uighur secessionists after several clashes, bombings and assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders seen as pro-Beijing.
However, the Central Asian states are sensitive to pressure from China, with whom they and Russia plan to sign a troop-reduction pact along their common borders next month.
Some Uighur exiles believe that may make them unwelcome.
"We will probably have to set up our headquarters in Istanbul or Germany," Khozhamberdi told the congress.
